name: Calcium-D-glucarate

card.summary: A glucaric acid salt sold to help the body clear estrogen; the evidence is mostly rodent work from the 1980s and 90s.
card.note: Supporting data are largely animal studies; human evidence for the estrogen-clearance claim is limited.

quick.overview:
Calcium-D-glucarate is the calcium salt of glucaric acid, a sugar acid found naturally in fruits and vegetables. Supplement sellers promote it as a way to support clearance of estrogens and other substances the liver tags for removal.

Most of the supporting research is in rodents, often in cancer-prevention models. No published trial was found that tests it for appearance or physique outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is that the salt yields D-glucaro-1,4-lactone, which inhibits beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme that can undo the liver's glucuronidation of compounds including estrogens, so that they are reabsorbed rather than excreted [1][2]. A 1997 rat study followed the formation and excretion of this lactone after oral dosing of a glucarate salt [2].
quick.risks: Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as generally well tolerated, with mild digestive upset, and advises that pregnancy and breastfeeding are contraindicated and that it may speed clearance of drugs removed by glucuronidation [3]. Treat that as unverified; no regulatory warnings were found in the sources.

lead: Calcium D-glucarate is a salt of glucaric acid (saccharic acid), a sugar acid that occurs naturally in fruits and vegetables. Glucarate salts are used in dietary supplements as precursors to D-glucaro-1,4-lactone, described as an inhibitor of the enzyme beta-glucuronidase [4].

In bodybuilding and hormone-management circles, it is promoted as supporting estrogen clearance. The scientific literature on it consists mainly of rodent studies of chemical carcinogenesis, beginning in the 1980s, in which dietary glucarate reduced tumour development [5][6].
No clinical studies of calcium D-glucarate for appearance outcomes were found. Wikipedia notes that more clinical research is needed to confirm health effects in humans [4].
infobox: Sold as a dietary supplement in the US [3]

paras: In the liver, many compounds, including estrogens, are conjugated to glucuronic acid for excretion. Gut bacteria produce beta-glucuronidase, which can cleave that conjugate and allow reabsorption. Proponents say that inhibiting this enzyme with glucaro-1,4-lactone increases elimination [3][5].

A rat study reported that D-glucaro-1,4-lactone forms in vivo after oral dosing of a glucarate salt and tracked its uptake by organs and excretion [2]. A 1986 study using serum beta-glucuronidase activity as a marker found that dietary calcium glucarate acted as a slow-release source of the lactone in rats [5].

In a 1986 rat model of chemically induced mammary tumours, a calcium glucarate-supplemented diet given after the carcinogen was reported to inhibit tumour development by more than 70 percent [5]. Later animal and cell studies examined skin tumours in mice, where glucarate was tested with other phytochemicals [6], and apoptosis in carcinogen-exposed mouse skin [7]. Review literature discusses glucarate among agents examined for cancer prevention [8].

For context, Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a placebo-controlled trial of 68 women using a combination product that included calcium D-glucarate, and describes human evidence as limited, with no large phase 3 trials or meta-analyses [3]. That description is not independently verified here.

Grokipedia states that the supplement is generally well tolerated, that it is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding because of insufficient data, and that it may increase clearance of drugs eliminated by glucuronidation [3]. The Wikipedia article on glucaric acid gives hazard data only for the pure chemical, not for supplement use [4].

timeline.event: Rat studies report that dietary calcium glucarate inhibits chemically induced mammary tumour development [5].
A rat study tracks formation, uptake and excretion of D-glucaro-1,4-lactone after oral glucarate dosing [2].
